summary: Solid, sourced, family-friendly core exists for a 7-10 sentence beginner story. Kukulkan (K'uk'ulkan) is the Maya feathered serpent. His pyramid at Chichen Itza, El Castillo, has four stairways of about 91 steps each (364, or 365 counting the top platform, matching the days of the year). On the spring and autumn equinoxes, in the late afternoon (about 3 pm), the sun makes a row of triangle shadows on the north stairway that look like a snake slowly sliding down to the carved stone serpent head at the bottom. INAH reads this as Kukulkan coming down to the earth to help the fields and the farming year. Today thousands of people gather to watch it. The 'how villages remember him today' part is thin in the sources: the best supported angles are that the pyramid is a living symbol of identity for Yucatec people and Maya communities, that the nearby Maya town of Piste carves wood sculpture inspired by Chichen Itza's stone figures (arte pisteno), and that a few modern folktales about a snake boy and a snake that flew to the sun are retold by Yucatec Maya (found only in encyclopedic secondary sources, so hedge them). Do not invent village rituals for Kukulkan. The village rain ceremony Cha'a Chaak is for the rain god Chaak, not Kukulkan.
facts: Kukulkan (written K'uk'ulkan in Yucatec Maya, Kukulcan or Kukulcan with accent in Spanish) is the feathered serpent of Yucatec Maya tradition. Sources agree the name means roughly 'feathered snake': k'uk' (feather, also the quetzal bird) + -ul (makes an adjective) + kan (snake).

The same feathered-serpent figure is called Quetzalcoatl in Nahuatl (Aztec/Toltec) and Q'uq'umatz (also written Gucumatz) among the K'iche' Maya. Some sources say the Yucatec name is a translation of Quetzalcoatl; others only say the figures are closely related.
El Castillo (also called the Temple or Pyramid of Kukulkan or Kukulcan) is the main pyramid at Chichen Itza, Yucatan. It has nine stacked levels (terraces) and a small temple on top.

Height about 24 m (about 79 ft) plus about 6 m for the temple on top; square base about 55 m (181 ft) across. Built over an earlier, smaller temple that is hidden inside it. Dated roughly between the 8th and 12th centuries AD; INAH puts it in the Terminal Classic period.

Each of the four sides has a stairway of about 91 steps. 4 x 91 = 364; counting the top platform as one last step gives 365, the number of days in the solar year (Haab' year). The south side is eroded, so the count is approximate and the calendar link is an interpretation.
On the north stairway, the side-rails (balustrades) end at the bottom in stone heads of snakes. INAH says this suggests the north side was the main side.

At the spring and autumn equinoxes (about 20-21 March and about 22 September), in the late afternoon (about 3 pm; one report gave the equinox moment as 3:51 pm), the setting sun casts a chain of triangular shadows on the north stairway rail. They look like the body of a snake slowly coming down the pyramid until it meets the carved stone serpent head at the base. NASA, INAH and Mexico News Daily all describe this.

The effect is described as seven triangles of light and shadow and typically lasts about 10 to 30 minutes. It is best seen on the equinox day, but is visible on days around it too if there are no clouds.

INAH (the Mexican government's institute of anthropology and history) explains the shadow as the descent of the god Kukulkan to fertilize the earth and keep the farming cycle going. Other reports say it marks the start of the planting and rain season.
INAH describes Kukulkan as possibly a ruler of Chichen Itza around the 10th century AD who, after he died, was remembered as a god linked to the equinoxes.
What he stands for in encyclopedic sources: creation, wind, rain, storms, farming and life; a go-between linking the sky and the earth/underworld (a 'Vision Serpent' messenger in older Maya art).

Spanish friar Diego de Landa (1500s) wrote that a great lord called Cuculcan (Kukulkan) ruled with the Itza at Chichen Itza and that the main building is named for him; Landa says people disagreed about whether he came before, after or with the Itza.

In the Maya books called Chilam Balam (kept in Yucatec towns, copied in the 1600s-1700s) Kukulkan is linked to the founding of the city of Mayapan and to uniting the families of Chichen Itza and Uxmal.
The pyramid sits over a water-filled sinkhole (cenote), found in 1997 and confirmed by UNAM in 2015. Chichen Itza has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

A handclap at the bottom of the stairway returns as a chirp that has been compared to the call of the quetzal bird (acoustic study by David Lubman). Some say the Maya may have meant this; this is speculation.
Since about 2006 visitors may no longer climb El Castillo; they walk around it.

Thousands of people (over 7,000 in an autumn equinox report; over 15,000 reported for spring 2026) come to watch the equinox serpent each year, with an INAH/Cultur operation and music. Yucatan residents pay a lower entry fee.
Scholars call Chichen Itza and El Castillo a pervasive symbol of identity for Yucatec society, the Mexican nation and contemporary Maya peoples (Castaneda, OSEA).

The Maya town of Piste, next to Chichen Itza (about 6,000 people in 2020), is known for arte pisteno, wood carving inspired by the site's statues, symbols and murals; its Maya community also claims cultural ownership of the site.

Modern folktale retold among Yucatec Maya (secondary sources only): Kukulkan was born as a snake; his sister kept him in a cave; he grew too big to feed, flew out to the sea and made an earthquake; he shakes the ground a little each July so she knows he is alive.

Second modern Yucatec tale (secondary sources only): the winged serpent flew toward the sun and tried to speak to it; the proud sun burned his tongue. A related line says he travels before the rain god Chaak, his tail sweeping the wind and earth.

Village rain ceremony Cha'a Chaak (Yucatan Today, 2023 news): the whole village makes prayers and offerings to the rain god Chaak for the milpa, led by a h-meen; four boys act as frogs. It is a ceremony for Chaak, not documented as a Kukulkan ceremony.
variants: Spellings: K'uk'ulkan (Yucatec), Kukulkan, Kukulcan / Kukulcán (Spanish), Cuculcan / Cukulcan (Landa, old Spanish), Kulkulkán (NASA's spelling).

Name origin: most sources say 'feathered snake'. Charles Lincoln (1994) argued it relates to plant regrowth instead; a Brazilian follow-up thought this too radical because Maya dictionaries (Motul, Cordemex) give 'feathered serpent'.

Who was Kukulkan: Landa has a lord who came with or near the Itza to Chichen Itza and who was later honored in Mexico as Quetzalcoatl; Chilam Balam has a unifier tied to founding Mayapan; INAH says possibly a 10th-century ruler later made a god; World History Encyclopedia says a man named Kukulcan (perhaps 987 CE) is credited with founding or taking over Chichen Itza and Mayapan. Do not assert one date.

Equinox serpent: some experts say the Maya planned it for the equinoxes; others note no other Maya building marks equinoxes and the effect shows for weeks, so it may be partly coincidence. Duration and clock time vary in sources (about 3 pm to 4:30 pm; 10-30 minutes).
Step counts: 91 per side in nearly all sources; World History says three stairways have 91 and one 92 (=365). Most others say 4 x 91 + 1 platform step.

Folk story variants: snake-boy and sister in a cave (earthquake each July); winged serpent flying to the sun whose tongue is burned; Lacandon Maya (Chiapas, not Yucatan) tell of an evil monster snake, which is a different tradition.

Shadow description: NASA says the shadow disappears until the next autumn equinox; INAH 2026 research (search snippet only) says the lighting pattern on the balustrade follows a pattern all year, not only equinox days.

cautions: Village memory is thin: no source documented a Kukulkan ritual in a specific Yucatan village. Do not invent village ceremonies for him. Safe wording: 'people in Yucatan still tell stories about him' and 'many people visit the pyramid at the equinox'.

The snake-boy and sun-tongue folktales appear only in Wikipedia and secondary or tourism summaries with no named folklore collection; hedge with 'some stories say' and do not present as the one official story.
Cha'a Chaak and h-meen belong to the rain god Chaak; keep them separate from Kukulkan or mention Chaak only as a different character.
Human sacrifice: World History Encyclopedia and others mention it for the temple and the Sacred Cenote. Leave out of a beginner story.

Religion and death: Kukulkan is a god of living Maya and Mesoamerican tradition and also a historical-ruler memory; avoid saying 'the Maya worship him today' or that he 'died and became a god' as flat fact. INAH only says 'may have been' a ruler.

Contested: whether the Maya designed the equinox shadow on purpose, the exact 365-step count (south side eroded), exact time and length of the display, and Kukulkan's historical date. Use 'looks like', 'about', 'many people believe'.
Toltec/Quetzalcoatl direction of influence is debated; avoid saying who borrowed from whom. Safer: 'the Aztecs called a similar feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl'.
Do not say the equinox is the only day the serpent can be seen; it can be seen around the equinox in good weather and cloud can hide it.
New Age, Gnostic and neo-Aztec equinox rituals at Chichen Itza are modern and not Maya village tradition (OSEA/Castaneda); the adishakti 'Kundalini' reading is esoteric and was ignored.
Climbing is banned since about 2006; do not have characters climb the pyramid.
Lacandon (Chiapas) evil-snake version is a different Maya group and tone; leave out.
The INAH 2026 bulletin PDF was unreadable when fetched, so only its search-snippet content (arqueoastronomers' study in Arqueologia Mexicana no. 197) was used; treat it as unverified detail.
Landa's text could not be fetched directly (sacred-texts returned 403); his account is taken from search-result summaries, so keep it generic.
